title: 250,000 Pages Is a Joke: Claude's Riemann Hypothesis Proof Controversy Undermined by Mathematicians Themselves
excerpt: “The proof runs 250,000 pages”—the phrase that swept through the math world—has been admitted by its author to be just a joke. According to a November 24 report
content_html:
“The proof runs 250,000 pages”—the phrase that swept through the math world—has been admitted by its author to be just a joke. According to a November 24 report, on the 23rd local time, mathematician Levent Alpöge, who worked with Claude on the Riemann Hypothesis, posted on X, admitting he had “done some silly things” and responding point by point to the controversy sparked by the proof materials.

Huge numbers are his guilty pleasure

Earlier, Alpöge claimed to have found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude and turned it into Lean code. The public materials contain about 17 million lines, and the claim that the “text version exceeds 250,000 pages” immediately ignited the math and tech worlds. He explained that he often jokes about huge numbers, and had originally meant to signal exaggeration through the lengthy formulation of the total order relation on real numbers in the main theorem, but did not expect outsiders to take it seriously; his earlier mention of Yang–Mills “60,000 pages of junk content” was also a joke. He apologized for this and admitted that he had been afraid to go on social media these past few days, but found the internet memes quite amusing.

The code compiles, but it is indeed rough

Regarding the public code, he admitted it is full of a large amount of low-quality content—it compiles, but the criticism of its structure and readability is “completely fair”; only for hard-to-explain technical reasons was tidying it up harder than expected. Responding to criticism from mathematician Armstrong, he admitted that he once spent nearly a decade organizing the proof of a certain theorem, and that this time he also took a risky approach: most of the proof may be unnecessary and could be greatly simplified in the future. He stressed that the argument is only the raw input for constructing a mathematical definition—number fields do not yet have an H¹ object, so one has to rely on a complex argument to build the definition; he has always believed that a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis should be simple enough. The proof itself remains unshaken: Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative jointly stated on the 21st that the code has passed verification by the official kernel and multiple independent checkers.
